collections.name: Movement
collections.intro: Movement begins with the body, but it is not a collection about the body in any conventional sense. It is concerned with what happens through the body: tension, resistance, balance, momentum, vulnerability and release. Anatomy provides the structure, but movement is the subject. Across the collection, the figure is repeatedly stretched, folded, suspended, twisted and compressed. At times the human form is immediately recognisable; elsewhere it begins to dissolve into sweeping arcs, intersecting lines and accumulated marks. This instability is deliberate. I am less interested in recording a body occupying a particular pose than in capturing the physical forces that make that pose possible. Bodies curl inward and then reach outward. Forms appear protected by enclosing arcs while simultaneously pressing against them. Figures rise through fields of marks that seem alternately to support, restrain or pull them back. The surrounding line is therefore never simply decorative. It becomes another physical force within the painting. Negative space performs a similar role. In the more densely worked paintings, the figure appears almost engulfed by movement. In others, large areas of exposed canvas surround a relatively small body. That emptiness is not absence. It gives the gesture somewhere to travel.

artworks.title: Held Against the Current
artworks.description: The figure appears caught between ascent and resistance, its body constructed from sweeping lines that loop, tighten and release. Anatomical certainty gives way to rhythm: torso, limb and gesture become increasingly inseparable until the body seems to exist as movement rather than as a fixed form. The vertical field of red introduces a striking counterforce. Unlike the restless curves of the figure, it is solid, architectural and immovable — a boundary against which the body appears to turn and push. The contrast creates a tension between freedom and containment, motion and structure. Rather than depicting a single instant, Held Against the Current suggests movement accumulating across time. Repeated marks preserve the body’s search for balance, while the open canvas allows the gesture to continue beyond its physical boundaries. The work asks whether movement is something the body performs, or something through which the body briefly becomes visible.

artworks.title: Held in the Turn
artworks.description: The figure is caught at the point where movement becomes tension. The body folds and twists through a series of sweeping arcs, yet nothing feels entirely released. Each line appears to pull against another, creating a physical negotiation between restraint and momentum. The open areas of canvas are important: the body is not enclosed by its environment but seems to carve its own space through it. Ochre, charcoal and muted flesh tones give the form an almost anatomical quality, while the repeated linear marks suggest muscle, tendon and remembered movement rather than literal anatomy. A restrained passage of red emerges within the lower body. It does not dominate the composition; it sits inside it like a pulse — the recurring red thread that signals continuity, vulnerability and life. Held in the Turn is about that fraction of a second when the body has committed to movement but has not yet arrived: suspended between resistance and release.

artworks.title: Against the Pull
artworks.description: The figure rises through a body that seems simultaneously weighted and extended. The torso twists upward while the lower form remains dense and heavily grounded, creating a palpable struggle between gravity and muscular resistance. The sweeping contours follow the body’s effort rather than simply describing its anatomy. Cross-hatched marks build tension through the torso and thigh, while the surrounding washes and downward drips reinforce the sense of gravity pulling against the gesture. The face is almost withheld. What matters is not individual identity but the physical act itself — the body stretching, contracting and holding itself against an opposing force. Against the Pull captures movement as resistance: the moment when the body refuses gravity and, through effort alone, continues to rise.

artworks.title: The Body Remembers
artworks.description: The body folds inward, becoming almost circular — part figure, part enclosure. Its anatomy is compressed into a dense architecture of muscle, bone and repeated cross-hatched marks, as though the body is physically carrying the accumulation of what has passed through it. There is tension everywhere, but little overt action. The movement happens within. The curled form suggests protection and withdrawal, while the exposed passages of flesh prevent that enclosure from ever becoming complete. The muted browns, bruised purples and greys give the figure an almost corporeal weight. Against them, the small red line becomes particularly significant: a pulse, a wound, perhaps simply evidence that something remains alive beneath the accumulated layers. The Body Remembers considers memory not as something held exclusively in the mind, but as something carried physically — in posture, tension, instinct and the unconscious ways we protect ourselves. The figure does not tell us what has happened. The body tells us that something has.

artworks.title: The Arc of Becoming
artworks.description: The body is no longer presented as a fixed anatomical form but as a sequence of forces. Long, sweeping lines rise, intersect and return, suggesting a figure stretching through itself — simultaneously contained and reaching beyond its own boundaries. There is a particularly beautiful tension between the enclosed oval of the composition and the sharp internal diagonals. The curves suggest continuity and flow; the angular marks interrupt them with moments of strain, balance and muscular resistance. The body appears almost to be constructing itself through movement. The red line is more pronounced here. Rather than simply marking the figure, it travels through the larger arc like a current — a pulse of vitality carried through the movement. The Arc of Becoming captures the body not at the beginning or end of a gesture, but in transformation: the moment when effort becomes movement, and movement begins to alter the self.

artworks.title: The Point of Departure
artworks.description: The figure occupies only a fraction of the canvas, yet its movement seems to activate the entire space. One arm reaches vertically while the other extends horizontally, creating an almost cruciform moment of balance — the body poised between grounding and flight. The economy of the composition is particularly important. Unlike the denser works in the Movement collection, here the surrounding emptiness becomes part of the gesture. The sweeping upward marks carry the body’s momentum beyond the figure itself, while the faint trailing lines preserve the movements that brought it to this instant. The horizontal ground anchors the composition, but the red line deliberately breaks that stability. Detached from the figure, it becomes a marker — a threshold, perhaps even a destination — introducing tension between where the body is and where it might move next. The Point of Departure captures movement at the instant possibility opens: the body still connected to the ground, but already beginning to leave it.

collections.name: Monochromatic
collections.intro: This collection explores the often unseen landscape of male mental health: isolation, vulnerability, emotional suppression and the gradual erosion of identity. The figures are psychological rather than biographical. Faces emerge from and disappear into darkness, features scratched, obscured and fragmented, reflecting the difficulty of expressing an internal experience that may remain invisible to those looking from the outside. Working predominantly in monochrome, repeated marks, abrasion and exposed surfaces create a sense of lives that have been weathered rather than simply depicted. Small interventions of red recur throughout like a thread, a wound, a pulse, perhaps even evidence that something remains alive beneath the silence.

artworks.title: The Weight of Being Seen
artworks.description: A figure emerges from darkness, yet remains partially consumed by it. His face carries the exhaustion of someone who has endured more than he has been able to articulate. The work explores the particular loneliness of being visibly present while feeling psychologically unseen. The eyes look outward, searching beyond the frame, while the body appears to retreat into shadow. A thin red line traces the edge of the figure. Throughout the mental-health series, this line represents what remains: wound, nerve, lifeline and continuity. Here, it is fragile but unmistakably present. He has not disappeared. He is still here.

artworks.title: What Remains
artworks.description: A solitary figure turns towards the light, while much of him remains absorbed by darkness. His expression is neither dramatic nor defeated; it carries the quieter weight of endurance. The work explores the psychological aftermath of prolonged distress: the point at which survival itself becomes exhausting. The face is marked and fragmented, yet the figure remains recognisably present. The red line appears again, tracing the vulnerable edge of the head and neck. Across the mental-health series it becomes a continuous thread — wound, pulse, connection and life. It is the part that refuses to disappear. What Remains is not a portrait of defeat. It is about the fragile persistence of self when almost everything by which we once defined ourselves has been stripped away. Something remains. Sometimes, that is enough.

artworks.title: Still Here
artworks.description: The figure appears caught between presence and disappearance. Parts of the face are sharply visible while others seem to be absorbed into the darkness surrounding him. Still Here explores the exhaustion of enduring mental distress when identity, confidence and connection have begun to erode. There is fear in the face, but also consciousness: he has not disappeared. The red appears only at the edges, almost outside the figure itself. Throughout the series it represents the continuing thread of self — sometimes strong, sometimes fractured, sometimes barely accessible. This is not an image of recovery neatly completed. It is the more difficult moment before that: remaining when remaining itself has become an act of resistance. Still wounded. Still uncertain. Still here.

artworks.title: Under Judgement
artworks.description: There are moments when a decision made by others begins to eclipse the truth you know about yourself. Long before it changes your circumstances, it changes the way you stand in the world. Under Judgement explores that burden. The figure is not broken by a single event, but by the cumulative weight of being assessed, categorised and reduced to a finding rather than recognised as a human being. His expression carries resignation, disbelief and quiet endurance in equal measure. The red line descends from the throat — the place from which we speak, defend ourselves and tell our stories. Throughout the series it represents the fragile thread of identity. Here it suggests a voice that has been constrained but not extinguished. This is a portrait of what happens when judgement becomes heavier than understanding. Every verdict reaches a person before it reaches a file.

artworks.title: Silenced
artworks.description: There are wounds that cannot be seen. There are voices that are never heard. In Silenced, the face emerges from darkness while the mouth disappears beneath layers of paint. The figure remains present, watchful and fully human, yet deprived of the ability to speak for himself. It is an exploration of what happens when identity becomes overshadowed by judgement, assumption or the narratives of others. The red line interrupts the monochrome like a pulse beneath the skin. Throughout the collection it represents the enduring thread of self — life, dignity and humanity that persists even when a person's voice has been diminished. This work is not about surrender. It is about the quiet violence of not being heard, and the resilience required to remain present despite it. The greatest loss is not finding your voice. It is discovering that no one is willing to listen.

artworks.title: Bearing Witness
artworks.description: Some wounds are too deep to be explained. They can only be witnessed. Bearing Witness portrays a figure who has endured loss, judgement and silence, yet remains present. His eyes are lifted, not in surrender, but in quiet recognition of everything that has been survived. The years are written into the surface of the painting as heavily as they are into the face. The red line cuts across the brim of his cap, disrupting the monochrome like a scar, a pulse or a memory. Throughout the series it represents the enduring thread of humanity that remains even after identity has been challenged and dignity tested. This is not the face of a victim. It is the face of someone who has lived through suffering without allowing it to become the whole of who they are. Every scar carries a story. Every survivor becomes a witness.

artworks.title: The Fracturing of Self
artworks.description: Trauma rarely arrives as a single event. It dismantles identity in stages. The Fracturing of Self explores what happens when a person becomes separated from the life they once knew. Professional identity, personal relationships, confidence and belonging begin to exist as disconnected parts rather than a coherent whole. The divisions running through the composition are not merely compositional devices — they speak to the psychological fragmentation that can follow prolonged trauma, grief and public judgement. Despite these fractures, the eyes remain fixed on the viewer. They become the constant that survives every loss. The recurring red line appears once more as the thread that binds the collection together. It represents life, dignity and the irreducible humanity that persists beneath shame, silence and adversity. However fractured the individual becomes, that thread endures. This triptych is ultimately about integration. Healing is not returning to who we once were, but learning to live with every fractured piece without allowing any single wound to define the whole. Identity can be fractured. It can be questioned. It can be stripped of titles, status and certainty. But it can never be entirely erased.
